title: Why We All Hate Avoidants
snippet: On attachment theory, Big Self-Love™ and the rejection industrial complex
content_html:
If you know anything about attachment styles, all I can say is I’m sorry. An avoidant has probably ruined your life. And to ease the emotional pain, you’ve intellectualised your feelings with pop psychology, wading through the rubble, reframing a wounded ego into an attachment diagnosis. Last weekend, I published a cultural observations episode about avoidants. Today, I wanted to write an article exploring it in more depth. In the attention economy, creating content often involves being a bit strategic. I front-load my videos with jokes to reel people in before hitting them with the social commentary, which is usually, deeply unfunny. I’m lucky I don’t have to be as calculated on Substack. No one on here has a sense of humour to begin with.

For the uninitiated, the Cleveland clinic defines an avoidant attachment style as a discomfort with emotions, a strong need for independence, and difficulty getting closer to other people. When it comes to romantic relationships, they freak out when things get real and ride away into the sunset, usually in their Volkswagen Golfs they’re not insured to drive because they kept putting off paying their taxes too. Avoidants are generally hated by anyone who knows them, because anyone who has had the displeasure of learning what an “avoidant” is, has usually been hurt by one. This creates a feedback loop, where the discourse around avoidants is produced and consumed exclusively through the lens of people who hate them. It would be a bit like getting all of your information about the Royal Family straight from the lips of the IRA.

Naturally then, in pop culture, avoidants have been vilified. They often get lumped into the same loose category as narcissists, fuckboys and bog-standard, entry-level sociopaths with a door-to-door sales job. They prove to be an easy target, because when unhealed, they can act out in irresponsible and selfish ways, hurting the people who fall prey to them. But the tragedy is: avoidants want connection too, just not as much as they want you to fuck off and leave them alone.

Before diving into a defence of avoidants, I’d like to delve into the individualisation of therapy.

When neoliberalism became the default way we understood ourselves, our inner world became coloured with advertisements, and slogans, and radical politics got overshadowed by radical self-acceptance. We became project managers in our own lives, instead of active participants. Every solution once found in your neighbours kitchen, was now to be found on the market, on a delivery app. When community fell apart, we all went to therapy, where we could talk about our personal problems instead of the social issues facing us all. We stopped living our lives with the public, and started living our lives in public; knocking down our bedroom walls and showing rhe world the inside of our minds. We lost our love of life for the lust of likes. We began to become main characters, finished products, and—dare I say it—content creators (sorry.) When we put ourselves first, no matter who else is sitting at the table, self-love came at the cost of loving everyone else. And this is what I call neoliberal therapy – when personal care mutates into a virus of narcissism. Now our main objective is to make ourselves a priority. The old machine of hedonism got doused in a new coating of spirituality. And we don’t recognise the same rusty cogs turning, they’ve become more subtle, and sleek after their wellness makeover. So now our capacity to feel good, and accept ourselves no matter the cost, is what marks the measure of a person. The greatest trick of neoliberal therapy, was to tell us that happiness comes from within, so we don’t need to create a better world for everyone to live in anymore, we can just manifest a better reality for ourselves. The most horrible people I’ve ever met, say they’re on a journey of healing and self-discovery. Maybe they should stop looking.

Big Self-Love™ has become the modern deity. It guides us, it tells us to trust our intuition, and intuitively, we listen to it, because our intuition told us to, I think… Big Self-Love™ wants us to maximise feelings of pleasure, while bypassing the pain. It will agree with whatever unacceptable shit we are doing, regardless of the consequences we inflict on others. Big Self-Love™ doesn’t need to absolve us, because there are no transgressions left to forgive anymore. The only carnal sin is to admit you have sinned, and that would mean you’re not perfect, which means you haven’t “done the work.” (prayer hands emoji.)

When you get dumped, attachment discourse offers a soft landing in the fallout. A therapeutic view of the world, can make us feel – for better or worse – like rejection, as a rule, stems from a fear of intimacy instead of a lack of interest; that they broke it off because they love you too much, and that the connection was so deep it ruptured their nervous system. That’s how much of an effect you had on them, because you – like everyone else – are a VIP. Big Self-Love™ doesn’t let us entertain the less palatable thought: that it might not always be their avoidant attachment. They might, specifically, be avoiding you. In the sewer of toxic positivity, anything that isn’t meant for us, won’t pass us, which means, we never really have to change as a person. We just need to manifest, and ask the universe to send us someone whose world will revolve around us because, now that we are omnipotent, we have a direct line with the universe and we can videocall her whenever we like, like she’s our friend who moved to Australia, and will just agree with whatever we say, regardless of context – and tell us we deserve better.

Big Self-Love™ makes an enemy out of anyone who doesn’t realise how amazing we are. So naturally, it implores us to classify avoidants in the same category as serial killers, or even worse, Russell Brand after he went religious. But through the typical flattening of nuance we see on the internet, avoidants have been categorised as wasters and fucked in the bin. And while a lot of them do in fact, belong there, the bin is not separated out by attachment style. When we start to condemn behaviour without understanding what created it, all empathy disappears and we treat our lives like a reunion episode of Vanderpump Rules; firing shit across the stage at the other cast members, and flinging drinks in the face of our rivals. I love that show. I’m going to watch it after I post this.

As humans, we are hardwired to look for patterns, and to seek out symmetry. We categorise everything to make our lives easier. We swallow the small print of complex behaviours, and use the label as a way to glass our enemies. But when we do this, we forget that insecure attachment wasn’t created in a vacuum, it often stems from childhood trauma, neglect and abuse. Many avoidants aren’t bad people, they just don’t have the self-awareness to do better, and are trying to cope in whatever way they can. They’re afraid if they fall in love they’ll hit their head, and lose their independence, and then the life they had will fall out of their back pocket, and their thoughts will leak out of the bottle, and they’ll misplace their train ticket to singlesville. Somewhere along the way, somebody taught them that to be attached, is to be let down. So they let go of your hand before you pull it away, because they don’t want to get abandoned again, so they’ll leave you before you get the chance to leave them. Their inward fear causes outward pain, when the love that they want is the love that they dread. But when all we can see is the consequence of their actions – we’re well primed to make monsters out of them.
